The LHCb collaboration at the Compact LHC has conducted a study of B_s^0 meson oscillations by analyzing D^+ -> K^+ B_s^0 final states. Leveraging these observations, I present the first-ever measurements of B_s^0 -> mu^+ mu^- and B_s^0 -> pi^0 mu^+ mu^- lifetimes. These precise determinations of B_s^0 decay characteristics and related decay rates are crucial for probing and restricting the scope of theoretical models that extend beyond the Standard Model.

This study establishes the complete classifications for nilpotent and solvable algebras within dimensions up to six under the Zinbiel structure. Furthermore, general nilpotivity criteria are formulated to apply universally. These findings indicate a direct correspondence between nilpotent Zinbiel algebras and a specific layered construction involving truncated generalized Pascal algebras, while all solvable variants can be characterized as extensions of the upper-enumerated solvable models.

The formation of the quark-glomn plasma, a novel state of matter characterized by minimal shear viscosity to entropy density ratio ($\eta/s$), occurs in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Investigating these collisions via multi-probe methods allows for the extraction of $\eta/s$ by examining both bulk thermodynamic variables and microscopic flow fluctuations. This study employs an ideal fluid dynamic framework to analyze the correlation between these factors and $\eta/s$, utilizing ideal hydrodynamics as a foundational reference. Although non-ideal fluid dynamics are necessary for a complete description, the research investigates whether certain flow fluctuation observables can more reliably reflect thermodynamic and transport properties or $\eta/s$ specifically.

To explore this, the research utilizes the integrated Bayesian heavy-ion analysis (iPHE), leveraging recent Bayesian prior distributions derived from the iPHE collaboration. The analysis demonstrates that fluctuations in elliptic flow ($v_2$) serve as robust indicators of $\eta/s$ and remain reliable constraints within an expanded, Bayesian-informed framework that expands beyond previous iterations.

Furthermore, the revised analysis identifies potential sources of uncertainty related to initial conditions and finds that variations in the proton-to-proton total inelastic cross-section ($\sigma_{pp}^{ch,in}$) significantly impact Bayesian results. Consistently answering queries over data with uncertainties is crucial in various fields, yet existing methods often fall short by either failing to represent all data semantically or failing to provide invariant query results across different data representations. This paper introduces an scalable approach utilizing $S_\infty$, the most standard four-valued logic, to achieve data-level consistency. Empirical results demonstrate that this technique correctly responds to $\textsf{CQ}\limits^{\pigo}$ queries—conjunctions of known truths unknowns—linearly with respect to the database volume, ensuring both correctness and performance.

Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs) have recently gained prominence for encoding complex robotic manipulations into compact representations by mapping end-to-end trajectories to object-centric descriptors. Although NDFs excel at transferring generalization to novel objects, they still require substantial training data, even for the simplest operations. Unlike the purely object-centered focus of NDFs, our approach utilizes a hybrid representation combining both object and task components. By leveraging this dual structure, we can achieve the generalization of tasks beyond the specific scenarios of initial training.

This work investigates the convergence of Approximate Message Passing (AMP) for the Zar2-synchronization problem, where the objective is to recover a special orthogonal group matrix from vector-vector products. Leveraging the connection between sample complexity in this setting and the TAP (Thouless-Anderson-Poliakov) free energy, we identify a specific instance of a global minimizer of the TAP free energy at inverse temperature $\beta=1$. Utilating this TAP solution at precisely $\beta=2$, we construct a sequence of positive definite inverse temperature values starting from 2 that converges in the sense of TAP free energy local minimality (note: original said convergence of AMP algorithm which is linked to TAP free energy). At these specific parameters, the TAP free energy exhibits local minimality. At exactly these parameter settings, the study demonstrates that no other non-trivial solutions exist besides the consensus. Finally, for sufficiently large $\beta$, the paper proves the uniqueness of a consistent solution.

Wide-field photometry serves as a cost-effective method for monitoring atmospheric quality by detecting relative changes in solar irradiance blocked by aerosols. Because this technique yields relative, not absolute, data on solar radiation, it cannot on its own determine vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD); however, when paired with concurrent sonde or satellite radiances—themselves uncalibrated relative to absolute scales—it can effectively derive vertical AOD values independently of standard calibration methods. Solar irradiance at the top of the atmosphere is first estimated using these sonde or satellite datasets adjusted for geolocation. This estimated vertical TOA irradiance is then divided by the measured surface irradiance, with the resulting quotient providing the vertical AOD. On a global scale, this approach generates high-temporal-resolution AOD maps that are uncalibrated but consistent. When sonde or satellite relative spectral irradiances are employed, the photometrically derived relative AOD maps can be further spectrally corrected. Ultimately, these relative AOD values become absolute when the sonde or satellite datasets are calibrated, enabling the production of globally comprehensive, high-temporal-resolution AOD datasets with full calibration.

Object pose estimation is a critical capability for robots operating in unstructured environments, yet it remains highly challenging due to severe occlusions and out-of-distribution views. Addressing these challenges, we introduce ProGroup, a framework that enhances pose generalization by integrating occlusion-informed projections into the group-based refinement process. ProGroup initially refines both rotation and translation parameters by refining predictive distributions across six views, explicitly categorizing them based on their degree of occlusion. Subsequently, the model refinements along with the specific view selection are carried out using an efficient differentiable process. By effectively incorporating a targeted refinement strategy that accounts for occlusion, this approach ensures robust refinement even when the most optimal projections are obstructed. Extensive evaluations across three datasets—Object3D, OcclusionX, and CLEVR—demonstrate that ProGroup surpasses state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in handling occluded and out-of-distribution scenarios.

We introduce Jellico, a novel extension of the Graphical Lasso designed for estimating high-dimensional Gaussian graphical structures in data where variable dimensions far exceed sample sizes. While addressing scenarios with limited observations, this framework robustly handles cases where the total variable count reaches high levels. Specifically, our approach leverages variable partitioning into distinct groups and incorporates latent variables to reconstruct structures that might be missed due to restrictions imposed by the "p exceeds n" constraint. Consequently, Jellico enables the identification of structures involving fewer variables within a larger p-dimensional context. Furthermore, our methodology offers flexible control over model sparsity. Extensive numerical experiments and real-world analyses demonstrate that Jellico outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques regarding precision and recall in edge detection, while also yielding more accurate graph structure metrics, such as lower graphical mutual information (GMI) errors.

Comparing the computational cost and performance of various numerical approaches is critical for selecting the optimal setup for biomolecular simulations of size and complexity, such as the charged alanine dipeptide. This research presents a comparative analysis of measure auto-correlation functions (G(t)) derived from molecular dynamics simulations utilizing three distinct methods: Metropolis, Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK), and a novel hybrid scheme combining Metropolis and dynamics-based sampling (often referred to as "HBS" in specific contexts like alanine dipeptide studies - *Note: The original text says "HBS", which stands for a specific hybrid method; I will use the description from the text*). Results indicate that the performance ranking remains consistent whether using standard bond constraints or SHAKE-constrained bonds, with the hybrid method outperforming both the Metropolis and BGK approaches in efficiency. Furthermore, there is a significant difference in how these methods handle auto-correlation measures for systems employing Coulombic interactions under periodic boundary conditions; specifically, the Metropolis algorithm yields G(t) values that are systematically lower than those produced by either the hybrid or BGK techniques.

Multilayer networks are widely used to model complex systems, yet assessing how crucial individual nodes are within these systems remains a significant challenge. This difficulty stems from the various ways layers can interact, as well as how nodes on different layers can be interconnected. This study introduces an integrated approach to measuring node importance that explicitly accounts for both inter-layer and intra-layer constraints. We evaluate this new metric against established methods using several synthetic multilayer configurations with known ground truths. Furthermore, we apply the model to a real-world air transportation system with and without inter-layer connectivity to analyze how these relationships influence importance rankings. Our key finding demonstrates that inter-layer constraints have a major impact on a node's calculated importance. Finally, we observe that varying the strength of these constraints offers a flexible mechanism to modulate the role of cross-layer connections in the overall evaluation.

Surface seals are critical components in hydraulic actuators, and understanding their behavior is vital. This study numerically investigates the behavior of a surface seal within a hydraulic cylinder during cavity drainage caused by piston impact. Traditional drainage models fail to account for seal dynamics, which influence both drainage rates and pressure dynamics. The proposed model integrates sealer dynamics into the standard incompressible drainage framework to determine the self-pressurization resulting from the piston's motion relative to the cylinder wall. This "self-pressurization" creates a negative internal pressure that increases with impact speed, causing the seal to retract into the rod. Such inward movement restricts drainage, leading to reduced pressure drops inside the cavity. At sufficiently high impact velocities, the seal can become fully depressed, effectively isolating the chamber and preventing further drainage. Traditional, simpler models that ignore seal dynamics are unable to predict this self-pressurization phenomenon or the associated internal pressure profiles accurately.

We examine a theta-term coupling within $\AdS_2$ space combined with a massive scalar field within an asymptotically hyperbolic setting. Using a thin-wall approximation, we determine the spectrum of states carrying both scalar and $U(1)$ charge. The findings demonstrate that generalizing the Witten effect to this specific $U(1)/\mathbb{Z}_k$ context occurs in two ways: first, the discrete charge spectrum is generalized, and second, the presence of the scalar field induces a shift in state charges analogous to the $\AdS_2$ generalized Witten effect.

The long-standing mystery regarding the thermodynamic stability range and the magnetic switch in CuFe$_2$S$_2$ (cubanite) is tackled here using GGA+U calculations across varying Feynman-Schmidzsch (FS) occupations. Our results reveal a consistent match between theory and experiment: the predicted formation enthalpy versus FeS concentration, as well as the conditions triggering the ferromagnetic transition, mirror real-world data perfectly. Analysis of the electronic band structure indicates that FeS incorporation introduces new states within the Fermi level, directly explaining both cubanite's stable coexistence with rautite CuFeS and its magnetic switch. Furthermore, our study successfully accounts for the previously enigmatic stable rautite phase observed at high pressures, as identified by Gao *et al.* (2018). The continued presence of intragunsh bands in the optimized GGA+U structure suggests that the recent experimental switch from GG A + U to the higher order GP A + U might be responsible for the enigmatic high-pressure phase. The findings further suggest that the recently discovered high-pressure phase is stabilized by strong electron correlations.

A quantum dot embedded in an acoustic cavity constitutes a promising acoustic spin qubit architecture. By coupling to phonons, it enables energy exchange between dots and oscillatory behavior via acoustic modes, while coupling to electromagnetic light allows for control through Rabi oscillations. However, accumulating dephasing noise from the acoustic environment often restricts their scope and efficacy. We demonstrate that adjusting the driving laser frequency serves to correct this dephasing. By optimizing this parameter, one can significantly boost both the amplitude and coherence time of Rabi oscillations, thereby enhancing the system's controllability and robustness.

We investigate the intrinsic differences in using beam splitters versus parametric amplizers as triggers for single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs). Our study compares these methods based on two key metrics: the likelihood of achieving the reaction (success probability) and the statistical characteristics of the resulting quantum ensemble. Our findings indicate that beam splitters offer higher success rates but yield ensembles with poorer statistical quality, whereas parametric amplifiers produce smaller success probabilities accompanied by superior statistical properties.

The complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor, as defined in the Newman-Penrose (NP) formalism, can be expressed explicitly for every possible type of spacetime metric. In this work, we provide the full set of twenty-two coefficients (Ψ₀ through ΰ₁₉) for the Dilation, Dirac-Meshariyev, General Rods, and Schwarzian metrics.

Long-standing theoretical inquiries into the thermodynamics of macromolecules in liquid solutions remain unaddressed in current computational methods, which typically model a specific polymer by representing it as an ensemble of its constituent monomers. This study introduces a novel framework for polymer representation based on the spatial distribution of its end-to-end vector. We demonstrate that this continuous density description yields an effective Hamiltonian capable of reproducing both the real-space conformations and thermodynamic properties of macromolecules. This effective Hamiltonian serves as the foundation for all current high-throughput simulations, allowing such methods to treat polymers intrinsically, in contrast to the implicit monomer-based approximation standardly employed.

The architecture addresses the challenge of segmenting structures with variable scales while maintaining precise boundaries. DDA-Net integrates two key mechanisms: first, varying dilation rates within the encoder enable the network to capture tumor features of diverse sizes; second, attention mechanisms within the decoder automatically prioritize encoder regions most relevant to esophageal structures, reducing interference from surrounding tissues. Furthermore, building upon the original Unet design, the architecture incorporates **skip connections modified with a weighted sigmoid function**. This adjustment mitigates convergence convergence issues and prevents overfitting commonly associated with the unrolled Unet structure. Although the rapid advancement of neural image captioning offers promising support for visually impaired individuals, the current lack of standardized evaluation metrics and protocols continues to impede practical deployment. This paper introduces W4Cap, a comprehensive caption evaluation benchmark designed to bridge this evaluation gap. Featuring diverse real-world scenarios, including descriptions for blind users, W4Cap provides objective metrics and subjective assessments to gauge caption quality across multiple dimensions. Our collected corpus comprises 85,000 high-quality descriptions generated from over 3,000 professionally photographed images via collaborations with visually impaired community leaders. Offering a comprehensive and practical framework for image captioning that supports better development of assistive technologies, particularly for the blind, we hope W4Cap will advance the generation of reliable, human-aligned image narratives.

Tantalum oxides, specifically Ta$_2$O$_5$ in its amorphous form and the H- and P-phase polymorphs (P- and 0 phases), have attracted attention for their potential use in high-k dielectric applications. This research highlights the critical role of precise energy loss function calculations for validating experimental data and understanding electron transport mechanisms. A key finding is that incorporating local field effects and spin-orbit coupling is essential for achieving accuracy in these computations. Furthermore, we identified a significant discrepancy in the energy loss function at low loss energies when comparing the P-0 phase's P-0 structure to the GGA functional used for amorphous and H-H phases. This difference suggests that standard GGA may be inadequate for modeling the structural properties of the H-H phase. Consequently, future investigations into electron energy loss functions should employ hybrid functionals alongside more rigorous theoretical approaches, such as GW.

This paper investigates the potential role of online misinformation in counteracting geographical big sorts—specifically, the trend where individuals with opposing views segregate themselves into different areas. We introduce a model in which agents choose between locating in a pro- or anti-misinformation region, balancing the desire to surround oneself with like-minded neighbors against the benefit of accessing opposing perspectives (which currently requires navigating through supportive content—a process akin to encountering false information). Our findings reveal that while moderate levels of misinformation circulation effectively disrupt segregation by fostering mixed communities, excessive misinformation is counterproductive, as it drives agents seeking positive reinforcement to remain geographically homogeneous.

This paper investigates the variability of linguistic expressions within speech data used for semantic instruction, analyzing how diverse demonstration styles, variations in audio utilization, different subtask execution, and errors impact the phrasing employed when conveying a task's concept. We introduce a framework designed to quantify the distance between data pairs based on their utility for training embedding models. Empirical analysis using this methodology, conducted on a subset of the Microsoft Hotel Dialogue Dataset, reveals the following key insights: (i) significant shifts in embedding model performance stem from changes in demonstration types and the inclusion of extraneous audio information; (ii) performance variations attributable to subtasks or demonstrated errors are comparatively minimal; and (i) top-performing data subsets often diver substantially from the random baseline, which may be counterproductive. These findings offer crucial abstractions for establishing more effective strategies in transfer learning sematic tasks.

This paper addresses the optimization challenge within quantum field theory, specifically focusing on Euler-Arnold equations derived from the standard Schrödinger equation using the left-invariant Laplacian on a general Lie algebra. The central task involves selecting the algebra and the specific operator to maximize the canonical Hammett functional, defined by the ratio of the functional's numerator (related to the squared Hodge norm) and its denominator (representing the squared $L^2$ norm). These equations dictate an optimal path $\xi(t)$ within the Lie algebra. The functional's numerator remains constant along such trajectories, whereas the denominator decreases exponentially as $e^{-t}$. We examine specific instances of these equations, including those governing the complex Euclidean and special unitary algebras, $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(N)$, as well as the complex Euclidean algebra. Additionally, we detail a family of solutions applicable to the $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and similar structures, characterized by circular motion within the algebraic structure.

Although automated testing frameworks are available for many conversational systems, they remain underutilized due to the extensive manual effort required to construct and maintain test suites. Existing tools often lack the flexibility to handle diverse scenarios, forcing practitioners to build custom adaptations. To address this, we introduce OpenDialog, an open-source framework designed to streamline the creation of automated tests for dialogue systems through an interface that is both intuitive and efficient. We demonstrate its utility by constructing a comprehensive suite of approximately 1,000 tests for FraCaS—an annual parsing evaluation. This dataset enables the development of a learning-based approach for predicting code that executes these tests, achieving a code similarity score of 0.642 when compared to the existing FraCaS test suite using OpenDialog. Furthermore, a framework trained on our learned data can actually run the original tests with 94% precision. We release the learned model, the synthesized tests, and a tutorial on utilizing OpenDialog alongside this new suite at our project page.

Recent research has shifted towards learning user preferences within graph neural networks (GNUs) to generate diverse item recommendations, yet these approaches often overlook specific feedback on the preferences of the recommended choices. Addressing this gap, we introduce D4Rec, a novel method that integrates Gated Aspect Enhancement for User Preference learning (GAPE) into GNUs. GAPE allows users to provide feedback on specific facets of a recommended item—such as its price or functionality—and uses this aspect-specific feedback to refine their overall preference models. We employ a knowledge graph (KG) to structure these feedback dimensions. Furthermore, we developed a Graph Attention Network (GAN) to automatically learn new feedback types beyond those in the existing KG and embed them into the system. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that D4Rec achieves superior diversity in recommendations compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

We introduce a methodology for naturally deriving formulations with significantly lower dimensions than currently known optimal versions, applicable to several hard combinatorial optimization problems. This approach relies on identifying a specific geometric "exotic cone" within the projection of the formulation's polytope that yields the desired, more compact polyhedral description. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this theory by providing naturally arising separated polytopes for the Steiner Tree problem in graphs and the Balanced Subgraph in Matrix Multiplication (BMM) problem. Notably, for the BMM configuration, our naturally derived dimensional formulation is nearly as dimensionally efficient as the existing optimal one. Finally, we sketch potential extensions of this framework to the Job Shop Scheduling problem and the BMM-based Balanced Subgraph.

We introduce a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating deep learning techniques in MRI segmentation across various real-world scenarios. Leveraging the OASIS dataset and labeling protocols from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD), we synthesized 17 distinct MRI datasets to serve as rigorous "unseen" benchmarks. These variations include releases of the same subject over time, contributions from different research groups, additions of specific clinical pathologies, and individuals with certain conditions excluded. We invited research teams to submit predictions segmented "unseen" MRI subjects based on our collection of training sets. Furthermore, participating groups were able to train their models on our "unseen" data, though not share architectures or specific training parameters. Finally, we synthesized the results by comparing three distinct performance metrics. Our findings demonstrate that the makeup of the training corpus notably influences how well segmentation models generalize to new, unseen MRI inputs.

We introduce a framework for network-based multi-agent optimization problems designed to unify and extend recent research by offering a common language, key insights, and effective solution strategies. At its core, this setting involves a set of agents, each maintaining a private decision variable and private cost function, with interactions occurring only between connected pairs within a given network structure. Specifically, an multi-agent optimizer seeks to minimize the collective sum of these cost functions by finding a global optimal variable. We examine how solution quality and convergence rates are fundamentally influenced by the geometry of the underlying communication graph. Although individual cost functions may be non-convex, we demonstrate that the global optimization variable retains a significantly simpler structural complexity. Leveraging this property, we develop a decentralized gradient-based algorithm that converges to a stationary point under mild assumptions regarding the cost gradients relative to the network topology. Finally, we validate the proposed method through a multi-agent robust regression task featuring non-convex interactions between agents.

We introduce a multi-agent expansion of the Motivation Dynamics framework to analyze the rendezvous behavior found in both controlled and uncontrolled settings. We examine key elements, including the resulting state-space structure, a method for validating theoretical predictions, and the specific implications for both guided and spontaneous meeting scenarios. Through this research, we clarify how the resulting framework applies to human-human interactions, human-robot interactions, and specifically how it influences human-in-the-loop simulations.

In QCD, heavy quarks experience both color Coulombic and linear confining forces, leading to the $q\bar{q}$ meson states known as quarkonia. This work examines the impact of confining forces within a non-relativistic effective field theory framework, specifically within the EFT of Quark-Pair Creation (QPC). We demonstrate that the resulting confining term in the quark potential is linear, a feature that becomes essential for understanding hadron production through the mechanism of quark pair creation confinement. Within QPC-EFT, we derive the confining component of the quark potential as linear, an outcome required to explain hadron production via this mechanism. Furthermore, we show that the QCD string formation and breaking during hadron production can be described using a field-theoretic version of the quark pair creation model. This string-based QPC model successfully accounts for empirical data, including the parameters of open heavy-flavor mesons such as the $D$ and $D_s$. Finally, we introduce a novel version of the Godfrey-Isgur potential motivated by QCD string formation. This new "string potential" $D$-quark potential significantly improves the description of $\eta_c$, $\psi(2S)$, and other quarkonia within a non-relativistic effective field theory context.

We establish exchange principles linking the generalized standard OGS of the finite classical Coxeter type $B_n$ with respect to Coxonsons, both to the element's Coxonsons length and its Coxonsons length exchange principle.

We examine the one-dimensional radial hydrodynamics of galactic halos under the influence of baryons, dark matter, and an external tidal field within the context of an expanding universe. We derive the equations of motion and state conservation, solving them numerically with boundary conditions set at the circumgalactic medium (CGM) interface. Our approach constrains the external radius $R_{ext}$ and the CGM's initial conditions, utilizing the known cold gas content of galaxies alongside observed stellar and atomic hydrogen ($\text{HI}$) masses to limit the $R_{ext}$ and dark matter distribution, $\rho_{\text{DM}}$. We further argue that the density gradient at this interface, $\nabla \rho(R_{ext})$, must also remain bounded. Comboring these limitations allows us to limit the external pressure, $P_{ext}$, acting upon individual galaxies. We demonstrate that in a $\Lambda$CDM framework, this pressure, alongside the external tidal field, is fundamental for explaining the diversity in cosmic star formation rates, the scaling between star formation efficiency and halo mass, the distribution of satellite galaxies, and the properties of CGM phenomena such as circumgalactic absorption lines.

T centre ensembles in carbons-diluted silicon exhibit characteristic optical spectral diffusion amounting to approximately 20 microelectron volts at 1 Kelvin within an ensemble of roughly 10 to the power of 14 centres. This level of electronic and geometric heterogeneity among the defects suggests limited applicability in solid-state quantum technologies. We demonstrate that spectral diffusion decreases notably as crystal temperature rises; specifically, at 4 Kelvin, it is approximately half its 1-Kelvin value, reaching roughly 10 microelectron volts. Furthermore, spectral diffusion within a single T centre is one to two orders of magnitude lower than in an ensemble, registering between 0.2 and 0.6 microelectron volts across various temperatures and samples.

The selection of an object detector for a specific task is influenced by various application factors, while current research primarily focuses on improving detection performance. This paper aims to evaluate the impact of different state-of-the-art detectors on the same tasks using the same data. We utilize the Cross-Dataset Object Detection Benchmark (XDOB), which aggregates five distinct object detection datasets. Features observed in protoplanetary disks, such as waviness, vortices, and low azimuthal symmetry, are examined through the lens of early planetesimal formation theories. Although the exact mechanisms behind these protoplanetary system (PDS) structures remain unclear, they are noted for potentially accelerating the growth of embryonic planets into gas giant cores before the disk dissipates. Furthermore, such structures could facilitate the accretion and mixing of volatile-rich outer disk materials with dust in the terrestrial planet region. Three specific PDS anomalies are analyzed to determine their capacity to enhance formation timescales and alter metallicity: vortices, spirals, and non-axisymmetric modes. Our analysis concludes that while existing literature offers promising theories, more research is required to substantiate these models with robust observational data.

The BigApple energy density functional (EDF), initially formulated and validated for nuclear matter and finite systems using Meitner energy, has recently been extended to cover a broader spectrum of input data. This update incorporates results from intermediate and highly excited states by integrating predictions from inelastic scattering, compound nucleus formation, and fission processes. The expanded "BigApple EDF" retains its robust performance across diverse phenomena, covering the periodic table in both ground and excited configurations. Its applicability notably reaches highly excited systems, with recent studies focusing on phase structure within such excited nuclear matter.

In this study, we introduce and evaluate two novel, geometry-agnostic Molmer-Sorensen gate designs that exhibit strong resilience against variations in carrier pulse frequencies within an ion trap system. These gate protocols generate a global multi-qubit interaction driven by specific ion-ion coupling patterns unique to each ion pair. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed CNOT-like operations significantly enhance entanglement buildup along the ion chain when combined with Cuzak chains. Furthermore, we apply these improved Cuzak protocols to a distributed quantum sensing framework, achieving a sensor network that attains Heisenberg-limit precision on a timescale quadratic in the number of ions, marking a substantial improvement over the sqrt(N) scaling found in individual ion sensors. These mol-sorensen protocols are built around number-shifting CNOT operations and are optimized for trapped protons and calcium ions to achieve a 99.999% success rate, corresponding to a 50% reduction in entropy compared to unconstrained operations. The proposed schemes function across various architectures, accommodating both monolithic and extended setups involving ions or molecules. A key advantage of these protocols lies in their ability to produce entanglement between distant nodes without requiring intermediate steps, contrasting with current methods dependent on local interactions. GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ serves as a rare, isostructural many-body analog to the Dirch graphene, exhibiting a 3D Dirac cone at E. The electronic structure of this material was mapped out using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Our findings reveal that the formation of these robust 3D Dirac cones stems from the interplay between highly anisotropic copper-oxohydroxo hydroxide bonds and copper-chlorine interactions within the bilayer framework. Specifically, the surface 3D Dirac points are situated approximately 0.2 eV below the Fermi level and are not protected by crystal symmetry. Temperature-dependent and repeated measurements tracing the evolution of the 3D Dirac points were made by varying the sample's chemical composition and doping levels. Although surface 3D Dirac points show up clearly in bulk materials, future investigations are needed to determine the material's scattering mechanisms and potential symmetry-breaking phase transitions. This work provides the first definitive evidence of 3D Dirac electrons coexisting with many-body phenomena in the same system.

This work analyzes the current experimental limits and upcoming projections for detecting the decay $\mu^\pm \to e^\mp E^{*}$, where $E^*$ denotes invisible final-state particles. Existing constraints from the MEG collaboration are found to saturate the sensitivity frontier for 1-body muon decay into the visible sector, $\mu^\pm \to e^\mp \chi^{0}\text{(vis)}$, targeting the visible sub-sectors. At high luminosity frontiers like the International Linear Collider (ILC), luminosity of $1000\text{ pb}^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=250\text{ GeV}$ could substantially relax search thresholds for the invisible channels by a factor approaching one order of magnitude for the specific parameter space where $\Lambda_{\text{NP}} > 1000\text{ pb}^{-1}$, extending these results over a broad spectrum of masses up to $m_e/m_\mu < 0.994$. These future searches would also constrain the dipole moment operator coefficients $c_{\text{dipole}}$ by an order magnitude relative to current precision. Additionally, Drell-Yan processes producing an initial state radiated photon and an invisible pair, $\text{DY} \to E^*E^*$, were identified as a sensitive probe for this sector via missing energy signatures.

Neural models have demonstrated high efficacy across a wide range of natural language processing tasks, including translation and summarization. However, traditional $N$-gram models continue to deliver strong results on certain critical tasks like machine translation. This study investigates the potential synergy between neural and $N$-gram approaches. We introduce two innovations: first, initializing neural language models with parameters learned from $N$-grams, which yields performance boosts for translation and summarization; second, using $N$-gram probability distributions as a regularizer during neural training, resulting in measurable gains for both translation and text abstraction. Additionally, we offer a theoretical analysis of how these initialized parameters function as prior knowledge and examine their utility as a form of regularization.

We investigate the conditions required to generate sufficient primordial curvature scale-invarity, denoted as ${\delta}\mathcal{R} k ^{-3}$, to produce a scalar power spectrum that greatly exceeds standard predictions within an affine distance of logarithmic scale. This approach involves producing large negative values within the Bardeen potential, $\Psi$, during an inflationary period. We examine whether such a scenario can occur following an extended period of slow contraction. Our analysis demonstrates that, under a minimal field framework, a period of slow contraction can indeed generate the necessary, large negative values for the Bardeen potential, distorting it significantly. However, this effect alone is insufficient to create the desired large, order-one values of the Bardeen potential required over an extended range of momentum scales. We examine two potential solutions: first, altering the dependent variable by adjusting the Hubble parameter, $H$, immediately after the contraction phase to achieve a substantial jump in the bardeen potential; and second, generating an abrupt step change in the bardeen potential through a topological defect, such as global gauge symmetry. We demonstrate that both approaches can produce the desired effect of creating large, order-one values of the Bardeen potential on an extended period of momentum. If this phenomenon were verified observationally, it would serve as a clear signature for either a post-contraction $\Lambda$-driven phase transition or the production of global gauge symmetry topological defects during early universe cosmology.

This paper introduces a spell correction method designed to automate vote tabulation by refining Optical Character Recognition (OCR) outputs from physical ballot images. While current commercial recognition tools often achieve over 90\% accuracy, the remaining discrepancies can lead to significant errors in voting systems. The proposed algorithm offers a practical, cost-effective solution by first cross-referencing OCR results against known valid options for each vote category. It employs standard text mining techniques, utilizing a list of plausible alternatives to identify and fix remaining errors. Validation through real-world data from the 2016 United States Presidential election demonstrated that this approach elevates accuracy to more than 99\%.

The current study employs the atmospheric circulation model to investigate the parallels between Mars' baroclinic storms and Earth's climate system, where Earth's gravity is reduced to match Mars' ($0.379g_E$) and its obliquity is adjusted to match Mars ($25.19^\circ$). Despite Mars having significantly thinner CO$_2$-dominated atmospheres compared to Earth's nitrogen and CO$_2$ mixture, the simulated Mars climate produces wind speeds and circulation patterns nearly identical to those of the Earth-like scenario. Specifically, the Earth-like Mars Hadley cells are confined to lower latitudes, whereas Mars' naturally occurring cells typically extend across the entire globe. Furthermore, the study finds that Mars' baroclinic storms effectively transport heat poleward, resulting in equator and pole temperature contrasts that mirror the similarities seen in the Earth-like case. Finally, the Earth-like Mars storm dynamics mirror the baroclinic storms found in Mars' native atmosphere, confirming that these features are robust even under significantly altered atmospheric forcing conditions.

Active learning (AL) is an information-driven Machine Learning paradigm designed to minimize the number of labeled data points required to achieve high performance. Although these algorithms have achieved remarkable results on small-scale benchmarks like Office-Clip and SVHN, they falter when applied to large-scale datasets such as ImageNet. The primary reason for this decline in effectiveness is the high computational cost associated with actively selecting and retraining on subsets of data at every iteration. To address this limitation, we introduce Iterative Batch Active Learning (iBAL), an efficient framework that requires only one round of full-data training initially. Subsequent adaptations are achieved by actively selecting samples within specific batches, ensuring the model continuously improves. Experiments indicate that iBAL matches the performance of state-of-the-art active learning methods on ImageNet while offering a significant reduction in runtime.

We demonstrate silicon two-qubit logic gates based on phosphorus donor spin qubits, utilizing $^{31}\text{P}$ as an ancillary auxiliary qubit to mediate interactions between target spins. By optimizing the spatial positioning and magnetic tuning of this ancillary qubit relative to the spin pair, we achieve a median $\text{SWAP}$ gate fidelity of 0.91(3) across various control pulses, alongside specialized sequences that surpass the mid-circuit crossing point to reach $\mid\langle\Psi\rangle_{\text{PSI}}\mid^2=0.93(3)$ for the $\text{CSX}$ operation. Process tomography confirms these results, which significantly outperform current intermediate coupling mechanisms, thereby facilitating scalable spin quantum computing through altered silicon lattice configurations.

This paper addresses the challenging yet crucial tasks of power allocation and scheduling for orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA) dynamic time division duplexing (TDD) systems. The primary goal is to maximize system sum-rate by simultaneously optimizing uplink and downlink transmission schedules, along with user-specific power allocation and subcarrier assignment. To achieve this, the problem is formulated as a non-concave mixed integer optimization challenge. Leveraging dual decomposition, the authors introduce the $\textit{Block Coordinate Descent with Dual Decomposition}$ ($\textit{BCC-DD}$) algorithm. This innovative approach decomposes the original problem into smaller, more tractable components solvable via dual variables, ensuring the solution converges to the dual optimal gap. Furthermore, the method incorporates a novel dual variable update mechanism designed to accelerate convergence. Simulations confirm that the $\textit{BCC-DD}$ method significantly outperforms traditional traditional dual optimization and random heuristic algorithms in performance and efficiency.

Organizing training data by task has traditionally been a significant hurdle in multi-task and machine-learning domains. We introduce a Hamiltonian Neural Network (HNN) designed as a task-independent, parameter-free meta-learner that handles this automatic data structuring. This meta-learned structure maps input quantum data—specifically time-series measurements of initial states and their corresponding values—to the time dimension. By organizing data this way, the Hamiltonian Neural Network can accurately predict the unitary time-evolution operator.

To validate this approach, we conducted experiments on quantum molecular dynamics and Heisenberg spin dynamics using an LSTM-based hidden variable meta-learner previously introduced by the authors. However, in a broader set of experiments featuring various initial and final configurations from the MNIST and CIFAR-100 datasets, the HNN's performance lagged significantly behind the LSTM-based model. The study concludes that the HNN's inferior results in these expanded datasets likely stem from suboptimal time-series measurements or initial and final conditions, rather than the meta-learned data organization method itself.

We introduce AIDA, a dynamic and flexible multi-agent system designed to collaboratively advance one another's model performance through continuous, real-time interactions. In this framework, agents construct, refine, and refine each other's models by actively exchanging training samples and related meta-information. The most capable agents identify and recruit others by demonstrating superior model accuracy and reliability, creating a competitive yet cooperative ecosystem. Agent capabilities evolve based on how effectively they improve their peers' models. Benchmark results indicate significant improvements in both target membership accuracy and trust scores compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Augmentation techniques are crucial for enhancing data volume and diversity, addressing data scarcity and variability challenges faced by Natural Language Processing (NLP) models. Although existing studies have explored data augmentation for specific tasks like machine translation and translation, this paper introduces a generic, task-independent framework designed to automatically learn these methods. By integrating it into an evolutionary process, the proposed approach optimizes parameters to fit various tasks without manual intervention. Moreover, the proposed approach is evaluated on three distinct benchmarks, demonstrating that it not only achieves competitive outcomes comparable to state-of-the-art approaches but also successfully learns augmentation strategies that surpass those obtained via baseline optimization.

In 1961, R. Askey and J. Werma introduced a family of $q$-special functions known as the $q$-Gamma function within the theory of basic hypergeometric series. This paper provides complex analytic continuations of those functions and identifies several previously unrecorded relationships involving the $q$-Gamma function and its inverses along the real line, the positive $y$-axis, and along the famous Hankel contour in the complex plane. A new collection of relations is also established in the form of $q$-generalizations of the Euler, reflection, multiplication, and addition formulas of the Gamma function.

As demonstrated by these capabilities, the use of natural language for both execution and optimization results in significant improvements in both robustness and accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

The rapid advancement of machine learning across diverse domains has led to widespread reliance on data-intensive data mining. However, the sensitive nature of this extracted information has motivated the integration of privacy-preserving techniques, with differentially private (DP) data-driven model training emerging as a key focus. A significant obstacle in this area is accurately quantifying privacy loss, a challenge that becomes even more complex when data points possess interconnectivity, as is common in graph structures. This issue is particularly critical in DP graph data modeling, where the non-differential privacy (non-DP) linking of points results in output model dependencies on specific individual inputs, creating cascading privacy losses that affect connected nodes. This study introduces PrivGraph, a practical framework designed to accurately compute such cascading privacy loss on individuals within private DP data learning using non-DP structure. By employing a novel upper-bound calculation for privacy loss in DP graph data learning, the proposed method offers a tight approximation of actual cascading effects, which are otherwise difficult to measure directly. Furthermore, the authors evaluate the real-world impact of these losses through the lens of private DP graph data classification, demonstrating the framework's utility.

The completion of the five-year legacy data period for the ESA Gaia mission marks a pivotal milestone, establishing an extensive archive that is poised to significantly influence diverse fields of research, including the ESA Euclid mission. To illustrate the utility of Gaia beyond its own objectives and to underscore Synergy between Euclid and Gaia, we examine several hypothetical scenarios projected for future analysis. These examples encompass Euclid dark halos, large-scale structure baryon acoustic oscillations, and the NASA Panchromatic Hubble银河 Survey (PHANGS), demonstrating how abundant legacy data will influence their trajectories. Anticipated advancements leverage over a decade of *Gaia* operations across multiple fronts, encompass the NASA James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), with further integration expected from existing and upcoming surveys such as the NASA Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (GAIA).

We present a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme designed to overcome computational hurdles in simulating non-equilibrium quantum correlations found in strongly interacting systems. This approach yields far more efficient dynamics than traditional lattice Monte Carlo or lattice field methods by operating within a linearized framework. Its application to the quark-gluon plasma formed in high-energy nuclear collisions demonstrates a clear benefit: it achieves superior real-space resolution of short-distance correlations, such as those in jet formation and energy loss, compared to both hydrodynamics without fluctuations and those with standard stochastic noise. These quantum-generated hydrodynamic fluctuations are explicitly modeled as interactions with a specific bath, mathematically represented via a stochastic term in the operator equation of motion. To handle these stochastic components efficiently, we employ a lattice-based random walk algorithm. Crucially, this method preserves the equal-time commutation relations necessary for unitary time evolution and correctly yields the KMS thermal state in equilibrium, ensuring physical consistency.

Using the Antisymmetrized Molecular Dynamics (AMD) model, we investigated electric monopole ($E0$) transitions and the evolution of excitation energy within the $^{64}$Ni nucleus. Our findings reveal an enhanced $E0$ transition strength toward the Ni isotopic drip line, alongside a concurrent reduction in the $2_1^+$ level's excitation energy. This downward energy shift stems from a more neutron-rich environment increasing the neutron count, which in turn deepens the neutron $N=40$ subshell gap. Specifically, the gap expansion is driven by a strengthened monopole interaction between neutrons occupying the $1d_{3/2}$ orbital and protons in the $1f_{7/2}$ orbital. The resulting deepening of the subshell gap and the associated change in the mean-field shape act synergistically to lower the $2_1^+}$ state's energy. These mechanisms help clarify the transition in the excitation energy spectrum of $^{64}$Ni and provide predictive insights into the nuclear structure of heavier Ni isotopes.

J-K-fold cross validation extends standard K-fold technique by executing K-fold process J independent times, thereby aggregating outcomes from all $K \times J$ resulting splits to produce a final metric. This method utilizes the variances observed to decrease standard error while preserving computational efficiency. Empirical findings from two studies demonstrate that J-K-fold significantly enhances the stability of performance assessments compared to relying on a single K-fold run, even when J remains modest, with further results supporting a theoretical framework establishing the distribution of these aggregated cross-validation scores.

Despite their inherent lightweight design, student networks frequently suffer from inferior performance compared to fully trained models. We posit that the suboptimal learning of student architectures, rather than inherent limitations, causes this performance gap. To bridge this result-structure chasm, we introduce a self-trained teacher (ST-T), an architecture featuring well-trained peer student networks used to instruct the main student. Our empirical studies in computer vision and speech recognition confirm that ST-Ts substantially boost student achievement compared to conventional training methods; notably, in the ImageNet task, the ResMobileNet student achieved a top-1 accuracy of 74.6%. Furthermore, we offer theoretical insights into how ST-Ts function and conduct extensive hyperparameter analyses across multiple datasets to validate their efficacy and robustness.

We introduce Causal Elimination, a novel causal graphical model component designed to accelerate both optimization and inference within algebraic tractable functions over causal graphical models. This approach mirrors the role of Bucket Elimination in optimization and Clique Tree Construction in inference, but with a crucial distinction: whereas Bucket Elimination and clique-based methods eliminate neutral variables to speed up tasks involving many users, our method eliminates variables to facilitate the flow of causal influences among specific pairs or subsets. By facilitating targeted inance (often referred to as "seeing into the future"), this capability enables significant advancements in causal diagrams, including new algorithms for computing the high-level view of optimization landscapes (the "global risk function") over four-variable subsets and accelerating queries that involve changing two variables simultaneously. These algorithms not only offer efficient computational methods but also provide a foundation for efficient recombination (queries involving three variable changes) and efficient counterfactual analysis (fast queries that simulate alternative scenarios).

This study introduces a framework for modeling photons as non-linear particles to account for photon recoil in intense light absorption regimes. This approach yields a generalized convolutional formula that unifies radiation force descriptions across varying saturation levels, from the optically thin to the optically dense limits where recoil is significant. Focusing on atomic systems, we derive a consistent expression valid from high saturation throughout. Photon recoil generates a convolution of a rectangular function with a Lorentzian, producing a "fat-Lorentzian" shape characterized by a broadened width $\gamma$ and an enhanced area, effectively doubling that of the standard two-level atom. While the central area doubles, the outer area increases less dramatically, causing a relative thinning of the "fat tails." Although primarily demonstrated with atoms, the methodology extends to other non-linear media such as vapours, Bose-Einstein condensates, and solid-state ensembles. This unified framework enables more precise measurement of natural linewidths and is crucial for accurately predicting radiation force behavior in modern high-precision optomechanical and optically mechanical technologies.

The evolution of phase transitions within granular systems is typically examined through two mechanisms: frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming. By analyzing phase space dimensions across various models and by comparing them to well-established, experimentally verified cases, this review demonstrates that these jamging phenomena align with universal critical phenomena characterized by critical exponents. However, a significant discrepancy exists regarding the nature of transitions in shear jamming versus those in isotropic jamming; although both involve phase space dimensions, the nature of transitions in shear jamming differs from isotropic jamming, as evidenced by inconsistent critical exponents.

We provide an explicit formula for the central $ SL_2 $-commutant $ Z(\mathfrak{sl}_2) $ at the critical level and derive it in terms of the generators of the Feigin-Frenkel center established by Feigin-Frenkel and Reshetikhin. Using this expression, we fully determine and analyze the Hilbert-Poincaré series for the centralizer $ Z(\mathfrak{sl}_2) $ when applied to the standard module $\hat{\mathfrak{g}}^\lambda $ over the disk associated with a generic weight $\lambda$ with $ p=2 $ Clifford symmetry.

The widespread adoption of algorithmic systems across diverse domains necessitates that public sector actors comprehend how these technologies function, particularly how search engine algorithms generate and apply Web search outcomes. To address this, the authors propose a novel framework grounded in computer science theory specifically designed for search engine algorithmic awareness tailored for public sector practitioners. Although verifying the factual accuracy of individual Web pages presents significant challenges, ensuring the reliability of aggregated Web page results is arguably more difficult. Consequently, this article examines biases inherent in both algorithms and the curated data they process, utilizing evidence from empirical studies, industry practices, and theoretical models. The authors conclude by offering practical guidelines and research directions aimed at enhancing the quality of Web search results within public sector applications.

The proposed TeV-scale muon collider represents a groundbreaking high-energy physics installation capable of executing diverse particle production experiments. This capacity includes LHC-level searches for weakly interacting particles, multi-TeV probes of gauge and Higgs sector interactions, TeV-order investigations into electromagnetic and strong forces within the Abelian and non-Abelian sectors, respectively, as well as a high-luminosity factory environment optimized for rare decay measurements.

Rapid and effective sampling techniques are vital for compressive sensing photoacoustic imaging (CASPI). Although linear sampling methods are computationally efficient, they suffer from poor image contrast and suboptimal noise performance. This study introduces rCASPI, a novel sampling approach that integrates a rank-based criterion with an adaptive sampling pattern. Our simulations demonstrate that rCASPI significantly outperforms state-of-the-art strategies, including linear, BPS, and CASPI, by effectively enhancing point spread function (PSF) consistency, contrast, and overall image quality. Furthermore, successful application of rCASPI was validated in real photoacoustic experiments involving ex-vivo pig skin and live mouse models.

The paired-permutation test represents a rigorous alternative to the Monte Carlo methods for assessing statistical significance in the comparison of two metrics. However, its computational cost escalates factorially with dataset size, often resulting in impractical runtimes. Addressing this limitation, we introduce and analyze an exact algorithm that utilizes a lexicographic traversal of the permutation space, leveraging combinatorial structures known as combinatorial regularities to drastically reduce redundant computations. Our complexity analysis demonstrates that this approach is markedly more efficient than the preceding Monte Carlo strategies. Practical tests indicate it outperforms those Monte Carlo basises by several orders of magnitude when handling moderate to large-scale inputs, thereby establishing this exact method as highly feasible for real-world applications across a wide spectrum of data volumes.

Cartels in the freight sector, which once dictated tariffs, collapsed in the mid-20th century due to antitrust legislation and eroding market trust. This paper utilizes a newly created dataset spanning 1950 to 2019, comprising weekly indices for both tanker freight rates and shipping volumes across various crude oil routes. Employing cointegrated regression models, the analysis investigates the evolving dynamics between freight rates and shipping quantities before and after the cartel era. The findings reveal that while the pre-1970s period was characterized by stable relationships where one variable could predict the other, this predictability broke down post-1970s. "Post Newtonian" expansions are frequently utilized in analytical investigations of general relativity to describe gravitational fields through parametrizations of the metric that gradually approach non-relativistic conditions as the expansion proceeds. This article demonstrates the application of a specific "pre-non-relativ" framework grounded in the thin-shell formalism, which enables an analytical series expansion of both the static (1939) Schwarzschild and the time-dependent (1939) Kerr-Nyerth-Teukolsky (KTN) solutions. The resulting approximations, valid near a compact object's surface, are particularly beneficial for modeling strong-field astrophysical scenarios. Consequently, this methodology facilitates a more tractable analysis of interactions between gravitational objects, including those occurring in the strong-field regime.

The study investigates the hydrodynamic forces and associated momentum transfer acting on a cylindrical intruder moving sinusoidally through both dense granular and liquid environments. Utilizing discrete element method (DEM) simulations coupled with smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH), the research examines how intruder depth, driving amplitude, and frequency influence drag, which in turn is analyzed via added mass and virtual mass effects. A key finding is that the regime of motion critically determines the drag mechanism: free and hysteresis-driven buoyant cycles exhibit a buoyancy-dominated trend ($F \propto V^{1/3}$), whereas jammed regimes display a tectonic-like behavior ($F \propto V$). Furthermore, momentum transfer between the intruder and granular material was assessed via collision metrics, specifically the coefficient of restitution and contact duration. These factors were determined to be highly sensitive to burial depth but remain largely unaffected by amplitude or frequency. Ultimately, these results offer important insights into the mechanics of motility within granular systems.

Noise commonly found in intraoperative data, such as that derived from ultrasound, poses a significant challenge in accurately aligning organ models with intraoperative and preoperative surfaces. This paper introduces a robust surface registration technique specifically designed to handle such acoustic noise. The proposed approach employs a deep learning framework to map the raw point cloud representation of an organ surface onto a corresponding point-voxel VNet architecture. A key innovation of VNet is its integration of a dedicated registration sub-network trained via supervised learning. This network outputs a rigid transformation and a free-form deformation (FFD) grid, which together facilitate precise alignment. Additionally, the method incorporates a novel loss function combining Chamfer distance and a soft-ICP term to explicitly guide the learning process toward accurate motion estimation. We validate the proposed approach using a liver model trained on intraoperatively acquired, noise-heavy datasets. The study first evaluates the method through an ablation analysis and compares its performance against standard registration algorithms. In the second phase of evaluation, the approach is applied to predict surgical steps by registering live intraoperative surfaces against a comprehensive volumetric FFD grid.

Although recent advancements in self-supervised optical flow have achieved high accuracy, flow estimation through transparent, occluded, and dynamic surfaces in free space remains a challenging task. We introduce a novel method to estimate optical flow in free space that integrates a robust surface selection module and surface classification module. The surface selection module employs a surface visibility estimator to distinguish between transparent and non-transparent (either reflective or diffuse) surfaces. Subsequently, our approach applies appropriate optical flow methods based on the identified surface type. Crucially, for the category of transparent surfaces containing occlusions and dynamic structures, we utilize a deep oculation net trained under a self-supervised framework. Comprehensive experiments validate the method's effectiveness across various scenarios, demonstrating its potential for real-world deployment.

Neuromorphic circuits are advancing rapidly, yet the vast majority of developed neural accelerators focus on specific tasks rather than offering general-purpose solutions. This paper introduces the concept of a Pulse-Coupled Neural Network (PCNN) accelerator designed for general computation. We begin by formulating a comprehensive classification framework based on classification surfaces derived from linear and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), utilizing principles of phase synchronization and synchronization breaking inherent to PCNN models. Leveraging the low overhead of linear and multi-layer synchronization checks, the proposed classifier achieves accuracy on par with Advanced Neural Network (ANN) approaches while delivering significant reductions in both power consumption and silicon surface area. Evaluation results demonstrate that the prototype outperforms existing synchronous and asynchronous neuromorphic classifiers, offering a 2.33× improvement in energy efficiency and 3.53× greater area efficiency compared to top-performing neuromorphic baselines, along with 153× and 5.53× better efficiency in cycle count and energy usage respectively versus their asynchronous peers, all with negligible additional circuit complexity.

In this study, we examine how a robust magnetic field influences the equation of state for spin-polarized, non-abelian strange quark matter described by an effective Lagrangian containing non-leading order interactions. Our analysis demonstrates that within this spin-polarized framework, the non-abelian matter exhibits significantly higher energy densities and pressure values compared to the scenario neglecting non-abelian interactions. Furthermore, the critical chemical potential required for the spontaneous formation of this matter increases due the presence of intense magnetic fields, thereby delaying the transition from hadronic phases to the non-abelian quark phase. Additionally, strong magnetic fields induce notable modifications in the behavior of non-abelian strange stars, specifically affecting their mass-radius relationships and surface energy densities.

Application-specific system call filtering (SCF) enhances the security of interpreted languages such as PHP and Python. However, traditional methods relying on static analysis or manual configuration often fail to achieve comprehensive coverage for dynamic languages like Java, .NET, and others. This paper introduces Timeloops, an innovative, low-overhead SCM that leverages execution time constraints to block malicious system calls in interpreted applications. The approach imposes strict time limits on individual system calls and escalates the threshold as the application progresses through its lifecycle. Our evaluation of Timeloops using Python, PHP, and Erlang reveals that it blocks malicious activity triggered by exploits, outperforming existing solutions with significantly less runtime overhead. Additionally, our study explores the implications of timeliness in dynamic language programming and offers guidelines for configuring execution time limits to ensure effective SCM.

This research examines the decision-making processes within the 1990 FIFA World Cup, utilizing each fixture's comprehensive event sequence—ranging from standard play to fouls, free kicks, corner kicks, and goal kicks—as the core of the analysis. By formulating a Markov Decision Process (MDM) where states are defined by the specific combination of these events and actions, transitions, and rewards are established based on subsequent occurrences, a one-step lookahead model was created to evaluate the desirability of each event. This evaluative method varies by game context; for instance, in certain situations, the rewards associated with compellable actions, such as committing a foul or causing the ball out of play, surpass those of attempting a shot on target. Moreover, while the proposed modeling offers insights into typical gameplay flows, it explicitly acknowledges that these findings do not serve as predictive tools for predicting outcomes in future matches.

Full waveform matching is a viable strategy for integrating seismic imaging with image-based inversion methods. Among the variants, domain-time waveform matching stands out for its conceptual simplicity and mathematical ease; however, the resulting integral operator involves a time dimension that becomes computationally prohibitive for both storage and manipulation. To address this, we propose a convolution-based operator designed to streamline storage and accelerate calculations in both two and three domains through transformation methods. Crucially, the storage efficiency of this convolution approach is dictated by the number of sub-problems solved per grid point in the spatial domain. By leveraging redundancy in source contributions across the domain-time interval, we further developed source-based convolutions. This technique cuts storage requirements by a factor equal to the total number of sources compared to standard convolutions while preserving storage speed. Nevertheless, our evaluation reveals that the benefits of this last approach diminish in domain-times because the expanded integration complicates waveform decomposition into constituent wavefields required for gradient calculation in real space. Consequently, we advocate for domain-based convolution as the superior method, despite the increased gradient decomposition complexity in the spatial domain.

We investigate competition between two species, types A and B, within an asymmetric noisy voter model on a regular lattice where neighbors stochastically adopt types based on type-B proportion thresholds $\theta_A$ and $\theta_B$. Depending on the interplay between these thresholds and noise levels, three dynamical regimes emerge: type B extinction (for $\theta_A < \theta_B$), type A extinction (for $\theta_A > \theta_B$), and stochastic coexistence (for $\theta_A = \theta_B$). In the coexistence scenario, one type becomes extinct in its own domain but survives by invading the other's territory as an intruder; specifically, type B vanades as an intruder into region A when $\theta_A = \theta_B$, and vice versa. We detail the mechanisms behind this coexistence, including how type B survives in region A when $\theta_A = \theta_B$, and numerically confirm these findings using fluctuating interfaces between homogeneous zones in step-profile initial conditions.

In Data and Energy-Traffic Division (TFiet) schemes are proposed for DED2D systems to optimize user experiences regarding data volume, battery consumption, and transmission costs. The proposed TFIET framework operates in two phases: the initial phase handles the distribution of data traffic and power between open-source and closed-source apps, while the second phase manages data and energy allocation among users interacting with these applications using non-convex optimization techniques and a two-stage decomposition approach. The TFIET model dynamically adjusts the fraction of data traffic and energy dedicated to open-source applications based on user behavior patterns, battery status, and real-time network conditions. Numerical simulations confirm that TFIET significantly outperforms conventional baseline methods in balancing data access efficiency and energy conservation for all participants in the DED2D environment.

The rapid advancement in nanofabrication techniques has enabled the creation of high-resolution, complex electrostatic phase plates (EPPs) designed to correct chromatic aberrations in transmission electron microscopes. This study employs numerical methods to analyze the point spread functions of state-of-the-art EPPs, aiming to forecast their optical performance based on fabrication specifics such as fill-factor and pixel arrangements. The work compares two fill-factor concepts: a pixel array with a central aperture and a pixel array with an interstitial opening. Additionally, the effects of varying pixel patterns—including cross, diamond, chevron, and herringbone motifs—are examined. The paper highlights a significant correlation between fill-factor and probe dimensions, reporting that fill-factors rising from 0.4 to 0.6 result in probe size increases from 0.09 to 0.19 times the EPP pitch. While changes in pixel pattern have minimal impact on current density at optimal focus, the data reveals that off-focus currents are highly sensitive to these variations. The study concludes by demonstrating how the presented model can predict the temporal evolution of phase plate performance, accounting for factors like conductive contamination.

Orbital stability analysis is conducted for solitary waves in one-dimensional nonlinear Schr\"odinger equations, considering both the self-induced and externally induced field under the influence of an anharmonic oscillator potential. For such systems with an induced field, it is demonstrated that the condition for stability in the unperturbed case also ensures stability in the anharmonic scenario, guaranteeing a unique, non-degenerate solitary wave that is orbitally stable across all masses. Similarly, for the self-induced field, the problem yields a solitary wave with exactly one mass for which the solution is both unique and non-degenerate, with stability confirmed given the unperturbed field's stability. Finally, the number of distinct solitary waves existing in the presence of an external field is determined, contingent upon the stability characteristics of the unperturbed system.

We investigate the additive Galois module architecture of finite non-abelian wildly ramified extensions within the rational field $\mathbb{Q}_p$ at its local completion. Our examination establishes several novel examples exhibiting these structures containing $G$-orbits of elements with non-trivial stabilizers, thereby confirming long-standing conjectures previously proposed by Fröhlich, Malle, and others in the non-abelian context. As a consequential development, we formulate and analyze two new conjectures regarding the associated regulator concepts.

This paper examines the optimal search methodologies for neutral long-lived particles (NLSPs) at hadron colliders, categorized by the decay length into three distinct regimes: macroscopic, intermediate, and microscopic distances. We detail characteristic signatures and the most effective experimental strategies for each decay length category. Furthermore, we illustrate these frameworks by applying the three-regime model to the specific case of a hidden sector U(1) gauge boson decaying into visible sector NLSPs. This specific application allows us to define clear signatures and potential hunting grounds for such U(1) models across the full spectrum of decay lengths.

Recent advancements in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) suggest that translation changes reflect semantic variation, utilizing methods like NODIST to identify edits between net translations that produce equivalent target outputs. However, this study challenges the assumption of constant source input variance, arguing instead that variance is contextual and dynamic. We propose a contextual variance neural model (CovNet) designed to incorporate these input dependencies. Experimental results reveal that increased variance correlates with higher frequencies of NODIST edits and improved translation quality, indicating that increased diversity arises from distinct translation strategies responding to varying degrees of uncertainty regarding source context. Furthermore, analysis of political discourse over the past decade demonstrates a 3.33% increase in translation diversity, a change attributed partly to evolving contextual variance; supporting this, we observed a 3.33% increase in variance specifically. Finally, varying source variance is found to plausibly justify a 3.33% increase in translation diversity over the last 3.33 decades. Nuclear migration constitutes a fundamental process during the development of the neural retina, a structure organized in layers according to nuclear density. While previous hypotheses suggested that migrating nuclei self-arrange to form these strata, an alternative view posits that the asymmetric distribution observed is merely a byproduct of migration dynamics interacting with retinal geometry. To address this, we developed a simulation based on dense active matter dynamics, utilizing a coarse-grained model where nuclei interact via short-range repulsion and experience position-dependent friction. We demonstrate that the resulting migration dynamics accurately reproduce both the temporal evolution of retinal development and the final steady-state equilibrium. Crucially, our findings indicate a strong dependency between nuclear migration velocity and the future retinal architecture, leading to the hypothesis that modulation of migration speed by mechanical cues—specifically frictional forces varying with location—is the primary driver of stratification. We further propose experimental validations to corroborate these predictions.

This paper introduces a novel class of two-dimensional (2D) compressive sensing (CS) image acquisition patterns, defined by a structured 2D sampling grid governed by specific 1D periodic and non-periodic sequences. The proposed method, termed 2D Compressive Grid Sampling (2D CGS), is designed to enhance image reconstruction across various processing applications. To achieve this, the study formulates a new 2D cost function integrating a convex $l_1$ norm and a weighted non-concave $l_p$ norm ($0<p<1$). This cost function is optimized using an iterative weighted algorithm to minimize $l_1$ deviations from the measured compressed data. The underlying 2D CGS sampling patterns are generated via the $l_2$-norm minimization of the mutual coherence of the resulting 2D sensing matrix. Extensive 2D simulations compare the proposed approach against existing 2D CS techniques, highlighting superior outcomes through plots, visual images, and quantitative $l_2$-norm metrics.

In response to the vast daily generation of texts and the critical need for accurate computer text extraction, this paper proposes a novel Chinese ID card text recognition framework leveraging Natural Language Processing (NLP). These model capabilities are further validated through an analysis of a dynamic Faraday rotation protocol.

This work examines the action of a subgroup $\Gamma < \mathrm{Diff}_0(S)$, where $S$ represents a compact surface with negative constant curvature, on the interior $\mathcal{S}^o_ - $ of the set of strictly convex surfaces equipped with the $C^\infty$ topology. It is established that if this action exhibits a single orbit under $\Gamma$ that is both closed and properly embedded, then there exists a proper, cocompact action of $\Gamma$ on the associated Teichmüller space $\mathcal{T}(S)$, which implies proper cocompactness on the corresponding uniform lattice in $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{R})$.
