The notion of square-root topology, first introduced by Huang, Wang, and Bernevig in 2017 serves as a signature of higher-order Weyl semimetals in three-dimensional systems. In such square-root topological phases, the existence of higher-order bulk nodes ensures that surface states are confined to higher orders themselves. These bulk and surface nodes exhibit unique characteristics: bulk nodes remain charge-neutral and disconnected from Fermi surfaces, whereas surface states, while gapless, fail to connect bulk nodes and reside exclusively on the crystal surface, distinguishing them from higher-order bulk nodes. This paper presents the first experimental verification of square-root topology in higher-order Weyl semimetals through magnetic susceptibility and optical conductivity experiments focused on surface phenomena. Our experiments confirm a leading-order vanishing of the electromagnetic response function in surface states, providing definitive evidence for their higher nature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the previously observed spectral weight anomaly in CdAs$_2$ originates from a geometric Berry curvature effect inherent to these higher-order surface states. The combination of experimental observations and theoretical calculations offers conclusive proof of square-topological states and establishes a new experimental paradigm for investigating theoretical higher-order phenomena.

Data completion involves reconstructing missing entries from a partial-informed sparse grid within a unit square domain containing a rectangular void. Consequently, the direct method's total computational complexity is established as $O(N\log^2 \log N)$, reflecting the combined effects of iteration count, cost per step, and solver overhead for convergence.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved significant success, yet the inability of standard self-attention to adequately handle long-term dependencies remains a key challenge. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have recently garnered significant attention for their ability to handle graph-structured data. However, the diverse array of variants available often confuses practitioners, and many algorithms claim originality without offering distinct advantages. This work aims to clarify these methods by demonstrating that the vast majority can be subsumed under a single, unified mathematical framework. We establish a consistent notation and prove that traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks represent specific, limiting instances of the proposed generalization. Furthermore, we introduce a modular framework for designing GCNs, separating the representation of data topology from the rules governing neural transformations. Consequently, this approach allows for a structured exploration of existing literature and facilitates the construction of novel models tailored to specific tasks. The framework's utility is validated through experiments on graph classification using DGI and GAT on the Cora dataset, as well as relational triple classification using DGI and DCGE on the RE relationship completion task. Ultrasound elastography is a technique that maps tissue mechanical properties by measuring mechanical strain and stiffness through the analysis of deformation within the radiofrequency (RF) signal. While conventional methods typically rely on matching short segments of RF data using a regularized optimization framework, these strategies often assume a uniform displacement magnitude across all directions. In reality, ultrasound imaging is anisotropic, resulting in higher and more accurate displacement estimation along the lateral axis compared to the axial direction. To address this, the proposed "separable elasticity" method incorporates direction-specific resolution by solving strain calculations independently for each orientation. This approach assumes that lateral and mechanical property estimations are constrained by their respective one-dimensional (1D) optimality. Simulation studies and finite element models were constructed to evaluate the performance of this novel "separable elasticity" framework against traditional regularization techniques. Furthermore, the method was assessed *in vivo* on the livers of two individuals. The outcomes demonstrate that the proposed method yields strain and elasticity maps with enhanced accuracy in the lateral direction, aligning closely with the high-fidelity axial data already produced by standard 1D assumptions.

This study introduces a stochastic dynamic game between an unseen agent moving in a graph and a knowing agent operating in the same environment. The blind leader seeks to locate the follower using only reports from the agent regarding whether it has moved to the same location as the blind leader's current position. We evaluate two navigation strategies for the follower: one where they play openly, and another where they remain hidden. To make in-positions decisions, we compare a full visibility setting and a partial observability setting. We examine how the follower's behavior—whether reacting to repeated visits or maintaining an evasive stance—affects the blind leader's success. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of navigation difficulty under both observable and unobservable conditions. Our key finding demonstrates that partitioning the grid into larger states improves efficiency; specifically, when the follower adopts an unobservable mode and partitions the space, it significantly lowers the total steps required to guarantee contact compared to fully observable scenarios.

This paper investigates energy-dependent Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) for W and Z bosons in high-energy collisions, such as those at the Large Hadron Collider. We find that the W and Z PDFs exhibit an increase of roughly 1 GeV at mid-rapidity, a growth that saturates at approximately 1 GeV$^{-1}$ of additional center-of-mass energy. These findings confirm the validity of an energy-dependent correction framework within universal PDF evolution, previously suggested by W and Z data; this involves adding a term $\eta(x, Q)$ to standard initial conditions, which depends on the boson rapidity relative to the collision rapidity but remains independent of the hard scattering scale. The energy-dependent nature of the $W$ and $Z$ corrections aligns with theoretical expectations, whereas conventional proton PDFs typically do not incorporate such dependencies. Furthermore, a distinct difference emerges between W and Z bosons: while W PDFs are largely driven by universal $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\rm QCD})$ initial-state collinear singularities, these cancel in Z PDFs due to the Z boson's neutrality, leaving Z PDFs governed instead by non-universal real emission rates and virtual corrections.

This paper introduces Dynamic Separated Memory (DSM), which advances multi-relation learning by employing distinct dynamics models for each relationship rather than relying on a unified one. In many multi-relational reinforcement learning scenarios, an agent encounters various environmental dynamics that shift according to specific relations; while learning from this diversity is beneficial, these dynamic shifts can also mislead the agent. Existing methods risk poor performance if a single learned model is sensitive to such variations. DSM addresses this by enabling the agent to select and activate the appropriate relationship-specific dynamics based on current context. Evaluation in both a simulated boxing domain and complex multi-agent wrestling shows that DSM not only matches state-of-the-art flexibility but also significantly lowers computation costs compared to approaches with larger parameter sets.

Regularized Conditional Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks (rcWGAN-C) have recently demonstrated significant efficacy in generating images with diverse and high fidelity. This work proposes utilizing rcWGAN-C to generate posterior samples within Bayesian inversion frameworks. A key innovation involves formulating the likelihood function as a regularized conditional Wasserstein distance (rCWD) by integrating the real data distribution against that generated by conditioning on specific conditions corresponding to noisy measurements. In this context, the rCWD regularizer utilizes real data to enhance certain noisy measurements, thereby stabilizing the conditional density estimation for well-posed inputs while acting as a regression task with regression rate $\gamma$ for ill-conditioned cases. This framework is advantageous as it does not require explicit parametric assumptions for the conditional distribution, such as Gaussianity. We demonstrate this approach in two scenarios: first, a well-posed Gaussian deconvolution problem where the rCWD regularizer functions effectively like maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation with a specific prior; and second, a noisy tomographic imaging task where it successfully reconstructs noise using deep generative models without assuming linearity or Gaussianity for the conditional distribution.

This paper introduces a CP-Transducer, which couples CP-Attention with an attention-based character-level transducer. The innovation lies in replacing the quasi-periodic connection in CP-Trans attention with a cascaded structure resembling a multi-scale self-attention mechanism. This adjustment enables the model to accurately capture quasi-periodic features, whether periodic or lacking strict periodicity. All experimental results using CP-Trans attention on standard corpus data confirm RNN CP-Trans attention's superior performance over standalone multi-scale or basic approaches in both spoken language and music classification tasks.

This paper presents a generalization of shadows, originally defined within strict 2-categories, to apply instead to $n$-categories for any integer $n\geq 2$. The extension preserves the topological Hochschild homology associated with a shadow and maintains the existing connection to traces of endomorphism operators in linear 2-$\mathbb{V}$-categories for $n\geq 3$. This generalized framework also subsumes various other definitions of the 2-$\mathbb{V}$-Hochschild homology.

Node feature-based Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have proven highly effective for node classification tasks on graphs with few labeled nodes. However, recent advances in GCNs that operate within hyperbolic geometry have shown even greater success by leveraging non-Euclidean geometry to better represent both transitive and hyperbolic characteristics found in graphs. A primary advantage of these geometrically aware models is their geometric inductive bias, which facilitates geometrically coherent embeddings of both nodes and graph filters. Nevertheless, current geometrically aware GCNs often fail to exploit the full flexibility of hyperbolic spaces, resulting in representations that lack an optimal balance between the transitive and hyperbolic geometric properties of the target graph. Furthermore, these works typically disregard the specific algebraic structures inherent to various hyperbolic geometries. To address these shortcomings, we introduce the Lorentzian Graph Convolutional Network (LGCN). LGCN is designed to learn node feature-based graph filters directly on the algebra of a Lorentzian group, enabling the direct construction of convolution operations within this filter framework. This approach allows the model to leverage the learned filters for efficient and effective convolution operations, ultimately achieving state-of-the-node classification performance across multiple datasets.

The applicability of the Tsallis distribution, characterized by the parameter $q$, to social systems has been examined. It is argued that this distribution arises from a nonextensive entropy ($S_q$) maximization principle applied to the stationary solution of a linearized Liouville operator. Within this framework, $q$ corresponds to the effective "temperature" of the system; consequently, variations in $q$ reflect changes in an individual's interaction with others and the time scales of those interactions. A application modeling the salary distribution of a workforce demonstrates these concepts, illustrating how varying "temperature" influences the resulting income statistics.

This work classifies unitary evolution into four types based on the existence and uniqueness of quantum equilibrium states: dissipative, dissipative with trapping, stochastically stable, and metastable. A corresponding Kramers–Kronig-Knauer (KKK) theorem is established to demonstrate the irreversible behavior of each category. Additionally, distinct non-orthogonality relations are defined between these classes and quantum Finsier–Landauer (FL) costs are introduced to calculate the minimum work required for unitary transformations. Together, these findings constitute a comprehensive irreversible theory of unitary evolution.

This paper presents a pedagogical introduction to negative temperature, conceptualizing it within a "two-level system" model where higher energies correspond to lower temperatures and vice versa. The discussion defines negative temperature mathematically using $dx$ notation, explores the process of "cannibalistic cooling" where hotter (negative) objects heat up, and clarifies why such states are theoretically unattainable on Earth. It also addresses why, despite the term, negative temperature does not indicate an absence of thermal energy. Finally, $dx$ notation is applied to model climate change, highlighting how rising global temperatures are "cooler" (more negative) as the climate system becomes less stable.

We investigate a dark seesaw model augmented by a minimal dark sector to demonstrate how vacuum instability and the potential breakdown of dark parity symmetry can be averted simultaneously. In this framework, vacuum stability is ensured by imposing a mass hierarchy, which also guarantees the preservation of dark parity at the point of spontaneous symmetry breaking. However, establishing this specific mass hierarchy creates a heightened sensitivity in the physical masses of the massive fermions against minor variations in the parameters of the theory. Consequently, maintaining a precise fit to current cosmological observations demands an exceptional tuning mechanism.

Effective spin-orbit coupling (SOC) is a prominent feature in various new states of matter, including magnetism, superconductivity, and topological phenomena. In this work, we introduce a spin-orbit liquid model tailored for 4d and 5d transition metal oxides. Within this framework, the parameter $\lambda_{\rm eff}$, representing the **effective spin-orbit coupling strength**, emerges from a balance of three key components: the original atomic energy scale, **crystal field splitting**, and **electron interaction effects**. Specifically, our approach treats on-site Coulomb interactions and **jellium** (the uniform background positive charge) in a rigorous manner while addressing the crystal electric field using a **perturbative** method. We apply this model to determine **$\lambda_{\rm eff}$** across diverse **crystallographic** structures, including cubic, tetragonal, and **orthorhombic** lattices. Notably, our findings indicate that a **strong** crystal electric field can substantially increase **$\lambda_{\rm eff}$** beyond the initial atomic SOC value. Finally, we utilize this model to analyze the electronic band structures of multiple **ir** (Iridium) compounds under varying **crystallographic** environments.

Diagnostic assistance via image analysis represents a crucial application of artificial intelligence. However, concerns regarding privacy and security often hinder the adoption of genuine patient data. Consequently, generating synthetic images using generative models serves as a viable alternative to address these challenges. Despite this benefit, current research lacks investigation into whether synthetic data retains the capability to identify and classify pathological features. Addressing this gap, we propose a framework that injects specific conditions into generated images by transferring latent conditions from real images containing actual disease markers. We evaluate this approach using Chest X-rays and retinal fundus images, demonstrating its efficacy in representing pathology within generated MRI scans of a dataset involving patients with knee conditions. Furthermore, we reveal that knee meniscus tears and knee osteoarthritis can be identified within the generated images with diagnostic accuracy rates of 91.3% and 93.3%, respectively, based on image analysis. This confirms the utility of altering latent space conditions in synthetic data for preserving pathological characteristics while simultaneously safeguarding patient privacy.

DaViDaExpert is a specialized data visualization component designed to help users perceive and navigate high-dimensional data within a 2D interface. Grounded in the Force-directed Graph (FDG) algorithm, it renders each data point as a node and adds edges between nodes based on correlations in a selected subset of dimensions. By displaying the resulting layout alongside dimension-specific tooltips, the component allows users to form an overview of complex datasets and comprehend relationships among data points. This paper presents DaViDaExpert as an implementation of FDViDa within DaViDaExpert, facilitating flexible, multi-dimensional visualization directly in DaViDaExpert environments. DaViDaExpert supports interactive exploration by enabling users to select specific dimensions to define data point relationships, thereby visualizing multi-dimensional structures in a straightforward, user-friendly manner.
